part_title: AgentCore Runtime, Memory, Tools, Gateway and Identity

scenes.title: AgentCore Capabilities
scenes.narration: This diagram is an overview of the building blocks around AgentCore Runtime. The agent runs in the central blue box. On the left, Memory stores and retrieves conversational context and durable insights, while Identity handles credentials and authentication for users and tools. On the right, Gateway exposes external tools and services through a controlled MCP-compatible interface, and Observability captures traces and metrics for debugging and improvement. Beneath the runtime are built-in capabilities such as browser interaction and code execution. Follow the arrows in both directions. Tool calls move outward from the agent, responses return, and telemetry flows toward monitoring. None of these capabilities implies blanket authorization. Memory retention, tool access, credential scope and monitoring should be configured for the actual application. The big takeaway is that running a model is only one production concern. Reliable agents need identity, tools, memory and operational visibility around the runtime.

scenes.title: AgentCore Runtime Deployment
scenes.narration: The five numbered stages walk through deploying an agent into AgentCore Runtime. Start with the source code on the left: your agent logic, tools, prompts and dependencies. The second box uses AgentCore Starter Toolkit or an equivalent supported packaging approach to prepare the deployment. Step three builds a container image with the required application components and pushes it into an appropriate container registry. In step four, AgentCore Runtime receives the configured deployment and provides the execution endpoint. Finally, the application invokes that endpoint and receives agent responses. Notice the CloudWatch box beneath the runtime: operational traces, latency and errors still matter after deployment. The orange warning at the bottom is significant. A managed runtime doesn't eliminate packaging and configuration responsibilities. You must review dependencies, permissions, secret handling and the runtime's supported interface. Test the agent locally, then validate it through the deployed endpoint before exposing it to end users.

scenes.title: AgentCore Memory
scenes.narration: This slide distinguishes short-term session context from long-term stored insights. On the left, the blue panel shows a conversation: the user asks about S3, receives an answer, and then asks for a Python example. Keeping recent messages and tool events in the session helps the agent understand that the follow-up still concerns S3. On the right, the orange panel extracts longer-term information such as a preference for concise Python examples or an interest in AWS storage services. Those durable records can be recalled in a future session where they are relevant. Follow the arrows from conversation to extraction, storage and later retrieval. The important design point is not to store every sentence indefinitely. Memory needs policies for what can be persisted, how corrections and deletions work, and when personal information should be excluded. Session context and durable memory solve different problems, even if an application ultimately uses both.

scenes.title: AgentCore Built-in Tools
scenes.narration: AgentCore's built-in tools give an agent capabilities beyond free-form text generation. This slide shows a browser tool on the left and a code interpreter on the right. The browser path lets an authorized agent interact with websites or a web workflow and inspect the resulting page state. Its example shows an application form with stages such as personal information, document upload and review. The code-interpreter path shows an isolated Python execution environment reading a CSV and computing a total with pandas. Follow the return arrows from each tool to the agent in the middle. The model chooses a tool according to the task, executes within permitted boundaries, observes the result and prepares its answer. These tools have different risk profiles: browsing may encounter untrusted content, while code execution must be sandboxed and resource-limited. Validate outputs, enforce domain and data restrictions, and log tool activity where appropriate rather than treating tool access as automatically safe.

scenes.title: Importing a Bedrock Agent
scenes.narration: This is a migration-oriented workflow. The first panel starts with an existing Amazon Bedrock Agent, including its instructions, action groups, permissions and knowledge sources. Step two imports or scaffolds that configuration into supported agent framework code such as Strands or LangGraph. In the third panel, a generated project appears with an agent file, tools, configuration and dependencies. The fourth panel emphasizes inspecting, reviewing and running that code locally, not deploying it without verification. Finally, the developer packages and deploys the adapted agent to AgentCore Runtime. The warning at the bottom is the most important part of this slide: importing is not a magic conversion that preserves every behavior. The team must review IAM, tool schemas, knowledge references, session behavior and the generated code. Build representative test cases to confirm that the migrated agent still gives correct answers and calls the intended tools.

scenes.title: AgentCore Gateway
scenes.narration: AgentCore Gateway helps expose tools to an agent through a controlled interface. Start with the agent on the left requesting the status of order twelve-thousand-three-hundred-forty-five. The centre gateway exposes available capabilities through MCP, handles authentication and credentials, and can support discovery of the appropriate tool. Follow the arrows to the right, where a registered OpenAPI REST API target receives the authorized order-status request. The external order service returns a structured response indicating the order has shipped. The gateway then returns that tool result to the agent, which can answer the user. The lower-right panel identifies potential target types, including Lambda functions and OpenAPI REST APIs, subject to supported integration settings. The point is to centralize and govern tool connectivity rather than giving every agent arbitrary direct credentials. Still apply least-privilege permissions, validate parameters and handle tool timeouts and errors.

scenes.title: AgentCore Identity
scenes.narration: This diagram separates two identity flows. The left blue panel shows end-user authentication: a human signs in to an application using an appropriate identity provider. That establishes who requested the agent operation. The orange panel on the right is about the agent or workload obtaining credentials to call an external tool. AgentCore Identity can help manage authorized tokens and credentials, including supported OAuth 2.0 integrations. Follow the arrow from the agent to the identity service and then to an external CRM or AWS service with a scoped credential. Notice the security cards across the bottom: centralized credential management, OAuth support, scoped access, and a reminder that AgentCore Identity is not simply the IAM Identity Center service under another name. A secure architecture distinguishes user identity from workload identity, passes only the necessary claims, and avoids exposing long-lived secrets in agent prompts or tool responses.
